books.section: Topic 2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

parts.modelAnswer: One way contact changed Native societies is that the fur trade created new inequalities: villages that trapped beaver grew rich on European goods while villages that did not fell behind. Trade made some villages wealthy and others poor, changing old relationships between neighbors.
parts.prompt: Identify one way contact with Europeans changed Native societies in the fur-trading regions.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for naming one accurate change, such as new wealth or inequality from the fur trade, dependence on European goods, or the spread of disease along trade routes.
scoring.notEarned: Naming only that Europeans arrived in North America, with no change to Native societies, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: One cause of the Beaver Wars was the decline of beaver populations near Iroquois territory as European demand for furs kept growing. The Iroquois needed new hunting grounds, so they pushed into Huron territory to control the beaver trade.
parts.prompt: Explain one cause of the Beaver Wars.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate cause, such as declining beaver populations, growing European demand for furs, or competition for hunting territory.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that the Iroquois fought the Huron, with no cause explained, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: One effect of epidemic disease was the collapse of the Huron: measles and smallpox killed between half and two-thirds of their people after 1634. The loss left Huron villages too weak to defend themselves when the Iroquois attacked in 1649.
parts.prompt: Explain one effect of epidemic disease on Native peoples in the fur-trading regions.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate effect, such as the collapse of the Huron, the loss of population that left villages unable to defend themselves, or the disruption of trade networks.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that disease killed Native peoples, with no effect on their societies explained, does not earn the point.

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing standard background on the fur trade, disease, and the Beaver Wars.
stimulus.text: The fur trade remade Native societies in the North. Beaver pelts bought European kettles, guns, and cloth, and villages that trapped furs grew rich while villages that did not fell behind. But the trade also carried disease along its routes: after 1634, measles and smallpox killed between half and two-thirds of the Huron people. And as beaver grew scarce, the Iroquois — armed with Dutch guns — pushed into Huron territory, burning their villages in 1649. Trade, disease, and war arrived together, and no Native people in the fur country escaped all three.
